Plain floor. Pip walks on it at its height.
The basic floor tile. Pip can walk onto floor at the same height and hop down one level, but never climb a ledge without a ramp.
Height digit 0-5 after the character (.2 = ground two levels up). No digit = height 0.
Build the shape first in ground, then raise tiles to make ledges. Height is where most puzzles come from.
Exactly like ground: walkable, pushable onto, same rules. It only looks different.
Takes a height digit like ground.
Use flowers to make an isle feel lived-in, or to quietly draw the eye along the real path.
Removes the tile. Pip can't step into the sky, and a crate pushed toward it stops.
Written as -. Right-click any cell to erase without switching tools.
Cut corners and holes out of the rectangle so the isle has a shape. The sky is a wall that reads as an edge.
Adds one to the height digit of whatever you paint over. Empty sky can't be raised.
Heights run 0-5. A pan's base must be 1-4.
One-level steps make one-way drops (Pip hops down but can't climb back), the simplest way to make order matter.
Subtracts one from the height digit of whatever you paint over.
Drag across a whole row to sink a channel, then bridge it with a ramp or a pushed crate.
A solid block. Nothing walks or slides through it. It stops ice slides, gust lines and glides.
Takes a height digit (the floor it stands on).
Put rocks where a slide or a push should stop, so ice has a landing spot and crates can't be shoved off the edge.
Same rule as a rock: solid, stops slides, gusts and glides.
Trees and rocks behave the same, so pick whichever fits the theme. Trees read well as soft walls along a path.
Water. Blocks, until a crate sinks in.
Pip can't enter water. A crate pushed into water sinks and becomes floor at that spot. A buoy pushed in floats as a stepping stone.
The height digit is the water's surface; a sunk crate becomes floor at that height.
Classic idea: one crate, one gap. Give the player exactly as many crates as gaps, so a wasted push means a restart.
Ice. Pip and crates slide until stopped.
Stepping onto ice keeps you moving in that direction until something stops you: a rock, a tree, a crate, a ledge up, or the end of the ice.
Takes a height digit. Crates slide too.
Make the player plan where a slide stops. A crate or rock placed as a "stopper" turns open ice into a precise puzzle.
Stairs. Climb one level toward the arrow.

The only way up. A ramp sits at the lower height: walk onto it in the arrow's direction and step off onto floor one level higher. Walking it backwards takes you down. It can't be used sideways, and crates never use ramps.
^ north · v south · < west · > east, plus the height digit of its low end. Click the Ramp tool again (or press R) to turn it.
A single ramp to a high goal is a natural "last step". Hide it behind a gate or a crate puzzle.
Pip's starting tile. It's ordinary ground afterwards.
Exactly one start per isle or map. Painting a new one moves it. Pip may not start where a hazard can reach.
Start the player where they can see the goal and what stands between them. The first glance is the first clue.
The glowing star. Reach any goal to win.
Stepping onto a goal clears the isle.
At least one. Takes a height digit, so a raised goal needs a way up.
Several goals are allowed, but one goal usually makes a cleaner puzzle. Raise it to make the climb part of the solution.
Crate. Pushed by walking into it.

Walk into a crate to push it one tile, onto the same height or off a one-level ledge. It can't be pushed up a ledge, onto a ramp or through an arch. In water it sinks and becomes floor. On ice it slides. It presses plates.
Sits on ground: the height digit is the floor under it. At most 8 crates and buoys in all.
Corners are traps: a crate pushed into a corner is stuck. Use that so a careless push costs the run.
Pressure plate. Pressed by Pip or a crate.
A plate is pressed while Pip (on foot or holding a stone) or a crate stands on it. Gates open only while every plate on the isle is pressed.
Takes a height digit. Buoys and balloon-Pip don't press plates.
Two plates, one crate: the player must hold one with their feet and park the crate on the other, then work out how to leave.
Gate. Open while every plate is pressed.
Closed, it blocks like a rock. Open, it is floor. It reads the plates at the start of each move.
An isle with a gate needs at least one plate.
Put the gate where Pip must walk off the plate to pass. The player then needs a crate to hold it.
Lever. Stand on it and press Space to flip every bridge.
Use (Space) while standing on a lever flips every bridge on the isle: up bridges sink, sunk bridges rise.
All levers flip all bridges. There are no channels.
Make the lever and the bridge far apart, so the player has to think about which side they'll be on after the flip.
A raised bridge is floor. When a lever flips, it sinks and can't be walked. A crate standing on a sinking bridge drops in and stays as a block.
Takes a height digit (the walkable height when up).
Pair one up bridge with one sunk bridge: every flip opens one way and closes another.
A sunk bridge is like water: Pip can't walk it until a lever raises it, and a crate pushed onto it sinks in and fills it for good.
Start a shortcut sunk, so it only opens after the lever. A crate sunk into it early keeps it open whatever the lever does.
Key. Picked up by walking over it.
Walking onto a key picks it up. Each key opens one door.
Sits on ground: the height digit is the floor under it.
Put the key behind the trickier half of the isle, so the door is a promise the player has to earn.
Walking into a door while holding a key uses the key and opens the door for good.
Keys and doors needn't match in number; extra keys are fine.
Two doors, one key: the player must choose. Make one choice a dead end.
Arch A. Step in to appear at its twin.
Stepping into an arch moves Pip to the other arch with the same letter. Crates never ride arches.
Exactly two p arches, or none. On a map, a pair on two different storeys is a gateway between isles.
Arches are great for "the goal is right there, but not from here". Hide the twin somewhere surprising.
Arch B. A second, separate pair.
Works like Arch A, paired only with the other q.
Two pairs let you build little loops. Make sure the player can tell the colours apart.
Sky Scales pan A. The heavier pan sinks a level.

Two pans hang from one vine. After each move, add up the weight on each pan (Pip 1, crate 1, stone-Pip 2, buoy −1, balloon-Pip 0). The heavier pan sits one level below its base, the lighter one level above, equal = both at base. Pip and crates ride along. A move is judged with the pan heights at its start.
Its height digit is the base, 1-4. If pan A exists, pan B must too. A pan can span several tiles, and the two pans can be on different storeys.
Park a crate on one pan to lift the other to a ledge you couldn't reach, then work out how to get the crate back.
Sky Scales pan B. The partner of pan A.
The other side of the vine. See pan A.
Base height 1-4. Can't be combined with water, ice, a plate, a crate, start, goal or key on the same tile.
Put the pans far apart so the player has to remember what's weighing the other side down.
Arch C. A third arch pair (maps only).
Works like Arch A and B, paired only with the other r.
Exactly two, or none. Maps only.
On a three-isle map, give each link its own colour so the player builds a mental map.
Balloon post. Space takes its one balloon.

Use (Space) on the post to take its balloon. Holding it, Pip weighs 0: can't push or press plates, is blown by gusts, and stepping off an edge becomes a glide, one level down per tile, landing on the first floor at exactly that height. Space anywhere else lets the balloon go, forever.
One balloon per post. Pip holds one thing at a time. Maps only.
A glide crosses gaps no crate can fill. Make the landing spot exact so the player has to count levels.
Stone pile. Space takes a stone, or puts yours back.
Holding a stone, Pip weighs 2: presses plates, sinks a pan, and can push a crate or buoy into the wind. A stone can only go back on a pile.
Maps only. Pip holds one thing at a time, so no stone and balloon together.
Weight 2 on one pan beats a crate on the other. Scales plus stones make good "which is heavier" puzzles.
Buoy. A crate on a balloon, weight −1.

Pushed like a crate, but it floats up a one-level ledge and never drops down one. Pushed into water it floats as a stepping stone that never fills the water and only the wind can move. It presses no plates and lifts a pan.
Counts toward the 8 crates-and-buoys limit. Maps only.
The upside-down crate: use it where a crate would fall the wrong way.
Gust vent. Blows light things one tile per move.

Blows along a straight line over floor no higher than the vent, until a rock, tree, gate, door, ramp, the sky or the edge. After each move every light thing in the wind (balloon-Pip, and buoys Pip isn't standing on) moves one tile downwind. A crate in the line shelters everything behind it.
n north · e east · s south · w west. Click the Vent tool again to turn it. Two gust lines may not cross. Pushing a crate or buoy into the wind needs a stone. Maps only.
A vent plus a balloon is a conveyor belt. A crate dropped into the line switches it off for everything behind.
Seeds never change the rules or par. The game also shows a seed par: the shortest clear that picks every seed.
Put seeds just off the short route, so collecting them is its own little puzzle.
Boulder ↔. Rolls east first, back and forth.

Every move is one beat, and on each beat the boulder rolls one tile along its lane, bouncing at the ends. If it covers Pip's tile (or swaps with Pip), Pip bonks and the move is undone. The game rings where hazards will be next. Space with nothing to use waits a beat.

The lane is the straight run of same-height floor through its tile. A lane of n tiles repeats every 2·(n−1) beats. Lanes may not cross, crates may not enter them, and all hazards must repeat together within 12 beats. Maps only.
Timing puzzles: make the player wait a beat (Space) or take a longer route to cross behind the boulder.
Boulder ↕. Rolls south first, back and forth.
Same as the ↔ boulder, rolling north-south.
Same lane and 12-beat rules as ↔. Maps only.
Two boulders on crossing paths are not allowed, but parallel lanes with different lengths make nice rhythms.
Thorn sweeper. Its arm turns a quarter each move.
The bush is solid. Its arm reaches two tiles straight out, pointing north, then east, south, west, one quarter per beat (repeats every 4). The diagonals are never touched.
With a thorn on the isle, boulder lanes must be 2, 3, 4, 5 or 7 tiles (12-beat cycle). Crates can't be in its reach, and Pip can't start there. Maps only.
Put a thorn at a crossroads: the safe direction changes every move.

Everything you have learned, on one mountain.
On ice, a push is a promise: the crate goes until something stops it.
The near pan sinks under you alone. Weigh down the other one first.
Crates can't take the arch. Whatever weighs the far pan must be set before you leave.
The pan at the top answers to the pan at the bottom.
One crate lifts the bridge - until you step on it. You weigh as much as a crate.
No push can lift a crate. A pan can - if it's loaded before the other side is.
The spring keeps the first crate it gets. Make it worth it.
Only one crate downstairs can reach the pan. Which one, and from where?
Load the lower isle to lift the upper one.
Stand on the post and press Use to take its balloon. Then step off the edge.
A balloon weighs nothing - not even enough to press a plate.
A stone weighs two. Take one from the pile before you ride the scales.
Buoys float up a step that crates can't climb - and they float on water.
Holding a balloon, Pip is too light to push anything.
With a balloon you can't walk into the wind. Quiet the vent first.
A buoy on a pan lifts it. Pip and a buoy together weigh nothing.
The wind carries the buoy. A crate in the gust stills the wind behind it.
Only a stone is heavy enough to push into the wind. Hands full? A pile takes it back.
Height is range: the higher the pan, the farther the glide.
The glowing ring shows where the boulder will be next. Press Space to wait a beat.
A thorn arm reaches two tiles straight out. The tiles between its arms are always safe.
Follow the boulder closely - and find a nook before it comes back.
Pulling a lever takes a beat - and the boulder doesn't wait.
A crate can't go anywhere a thorn arm can reach - not even into water.
Neither the boulder's lane nor the thorn's reach will take a crate. Find the one gap between them.
An arch catches whatever the ice carries, but only you go through.
Two crates, two jobs: one to weigh, one to stand on.

No account needed to play or build. Sign in only to share online.
Klarbase is a small open-source game made by one person. It collects as little as it can, sells nothing and shows no ads. This page lists everything that is stored.

Your progress (stars, best moves and times), settings, the isle you're building, your Daily stars and the GitHub name you type for exports are kept in your browser's local storage. They never leave your device. Clearing this site's data in your browser removes them.

To rate how hard each isle is, the game sends small events when you start, clear, restart or ask for a hint on an isle, with your moves and a rough time for a clear. The server only adds them to running totals per isle. They are sent without cookies and carry no account, device id or IP address, so they can't be traced back to you.
Signing in is only needed to share isles online. When you sign in with GitHub or Google we receive and keep:
name, email address and profile picture
from that account, and the link to it (including the sign-in tokens it hands us);
that keeps you signed in - the only cookie Klarbase sets;
it was started from, used to keep accounts secure. Signing out ends the session.
Isles you share online are public, with your name as their maker. Reports you file on isles are kept with your account.
When you send feedback we store your message, the page you sent it from, the reply email if you give one, and your account if you're signed in. No IP address is stored.
Visits are counted with Cloudflare Web Analytics, which uses no cookies and doesn't track you across sites.

The game runs on Railway, the database on Neon, and all traffic passes through Cloudflare. GitHub and Google handle sign-in. To protect the server from abuse, it remembers IP addresses in memory for up to an hour to limit how often one address can send requests; they are never written down.
The only cookie is the sign-in one, and local storage only holds your own game. Both are strictly necessary for what you asked the game to do, so there's nothing to consent to.

To delete your account, sign in and send feedback asking for it - that tells us the request really comes from you.
